note: What Squamish Wants: specific asks residents answer yes, no or don't mind. These are the starter asks, each from the public record with a source. Residents add more on the site (stored in the database by api/wants.js). status: none | plan | agenda | done | province. who: council | province. area: a neighbourhood slug from data/neighbourhoods.json, or null for the whole town. kind: 'choice' asks have options [{key,label,means}] instead of yes/no; everyone can also pick Don't mind (m).

asks.title: What should happen with people still camping downtown?
asks.why: The District closed the camp behind Under One Roof for good on October 9, 2026, after a fire in September. Some people moved near Vancouver Street and Loggers Lane. The Province’s temporary housing has no site yet.
asks.source_label: Issues we follow: Under One Roof

options.label: Move camps on now
options.means: Neighbours and businesses get the area back; people camping may have nowhere to go yet.

options.label: Wait until temporary housing opens
options.means: People have somewhere to move to, but camping continues until then (BC Housing estimates winter 2027/28).

options.label: Let people stay with more support
options.means: Outreach and services go to the site instead of moving people on.

asks.title: Put the modular shelter somewhere other than the park near Junction Park
asks.why: Residents petitioned in April 2026 for a different site than Xwu’nekw Park on Loggers Lane. Council took the park off the list in June 2026.
asks.other_side: Any site will have neighbours, and moving it can delay housing for people who need it now.

asks.title: What should happen with the supportive housing planned at 39900 Government Road?
asks.why: BC Housing plans six storeys with 65 studio homes and support staff around the clock, run by Squamish Helping Hands. Construction is set to start in summer 2027.
asks.source_label: Issues we follow: Government Road housing

options.label: Build it as planned
options.means: 65 homes with support for people leaving homelessness.

options.label: Build it, with changes
options.means: For example a smaller building, or more say for neighbours in how it’s run.

options.label: Build it somewhere else
options.means: A different site, which likely means a delay.

asks.title: How should Squamish help open more licensed child care spaces?
asks.why: In May 2020 council endorsed a child care action plan with a goal of 720 new licensed spaces by 2029. The Province licenses and funds most child care; the District can offer land or space and speed up permits, as it did for the 36 space centre in Valleycliffe that opened in 2025.
asks.source_label: District of Squamish: new Valleycliffe child care centre

options.label: Build or lease District space for daycares
options.means: More spaces sooner; it costs tax money or land the District could use for something else.

options.label: Only speed up permits for private daycares
options.means: Little cost to taxpayers; how many spaces open is up to providers.

options.label: Leave it to the Province
options.means: No local cost; spaces depend on provincial funding and may come slower.

asks.title: How should Squamish get more homes that people can rent?
asks.why: Rents are high and long term rentals are hard to find. Council decides rezonings for rental buildings, can put District land toward nonprofit housing, and since 2023 can waive development fees for nonprofit affordable rental homes.

options.label: Put more District land toward nonprofit rentals
options.means: More below market rentals over time; that land can’t go to parks or be sold to pay for other things.

options.label: Approve private rental buildings faster
options.means: More rentals sooner at market rents; neighbours get less say on each project.

options.label: Put tax money toward buying rental buildings
options.means: Keeps some rents lower; the cost goes onto property tax bills.

options.label: Slow down until roads and services catch up
options.means: Less strain on roads, schools and pipes; rents may keep rising.

asks.title: Install the defibrillator at the Brennan Park pickleball and tennis courts this year
asks.why: Pickleball Squamish offered up to $4,000 toward it. A June 2026 staff report scheduled it for 2027.
asks.other_side: The cabinet and data plan add yearly costs, and staff time is already planned for other work this year.

asks.title: When should Squamish build more pickleball courts?
asks.why: In March 2026 staff asked council to hold off on new courts until the 2027 Parks and Recreation Master Plan looks at racket sports.

options.label: Now
options.means: Courts sooner, before the 2027 parks plan looks at all racket sports.

options.label: After the 2027 parks plan
options.means: Courts go where the plan says they are needed most, alongside tennis.

options.label: We have enough courts
options.means: The money goes to other parks and recreation needs.

asks.title: Fix up the Eaglewind courts and reopen them for tennis
asks.why: The courts have sat unused since pickleball moved to Brennan Park. Staff recommended fixing them up for tennis, but in April 2026 council chose to explore other interim uses instead, not including pickleball.
asks.other_side: The money could go toward courts in a busier spot.

asks.title: What should Brennan Park add next?
asks.why: A second rink and a second pool are both in the District’s long term vision, with no money set aside yet. A task force report is due in 2027.

options.label: A second sheet of ice
options.means: More ice time for hockey, figure skating and public skating.

options.label: A second pool
options.means: More lane, lesson and leisure swim time.

options.label: Both, even if taxes go up
options.means: Big new buildings to build and run, which likely means borrowing or higher taxes.

options.label: Neither for now
options.means: Keeps that money for other needs or lower taxes.

asks.title: Fence the off leash dog area at John Hunter Park
asks.why: John Hunter Park is one of the off leash pilot sites. The District says it still needs a fence, with no timeline set.
asks.other_side: Some park users would rather keep the park open and unfenced for everyone.
asks.source_label: District of Squamish: off leash pilot

asks.title: Build covered outdoor basketball courts
asks.why: Residents asked for covered outdoor courts in the 2021 feedback on the Brennan Park plan, so they can be used in the rain.
asks.other_side: A roof adds a lot to the cost of a court.

asks.title: Keep the new crosswalk and wider multi use lane on Highlands Way North
asks.why: Done in August 2026 after concerns about speeding in the school zone: a wider multi use lane with a buffer, no centre line, and a new crosswalk south of Pentland Way.
asks.other_side: Some drivers say the changes slow a main route out of the Highlands.

asks.title: Put raised crosswalks and new signs on Upper Mamquam Road
asks.why: Speeding and truck traffic. It is the District’s top ranked traffic calming site, and two raised crosswalks east of Aristotle Drive are set to be built in late October 2026.
asks.other_side: Raised crosswalks slow emergency vehicles and are hard on trucks that need the road.

asks.title: Put a raised crosswalk and new signs on Skyline Drive
asks.why: It is on the District's 2026 traffic calming list.
asks.other_side: Raised crosswalks slow everyone, including buses and emergency vehicles.

asks.title: Make the Highway 99 and Cleveland Avenue intersection safer
asks.why: The District says it has the most crashes of any intersection in town. The Province runs the highway, so council's role is to press for changes.
asks.other_side: The Province added a lane there in 2022 and may not fund more work soon.
asks.source_label: District of Squamish: Highway 99 at Cleveland

asks.title: Should downtown parking stay free?
asks.why: A 2023 study suggested paid parking downtown. Council chose to test it at Darrell Bay only.

options.label: Keep it all free
options.means: No meters downtown; busy spots stay hard to find at peak times.

options.label: Paid only in the busiest spots
options.means: Short free time limits elsewhere; meters where demand is highest.

options.label: Paid parking across downtown
options.means: Frees up spots and raises money without raising taxes.

asks.title: Should Squamish help pay for a bus to Vancouver and Whistler?
asks.why: Squamish has local buses but no public bus to Vancouver or Whistler. It has been studied since 2015 and has stalled over who runs and pays for it.

options.label: Yes, even with a small tax increase
options.means: Squamish pays its share of the yearly cost through property taxes.

options.label: Only if the Province pays
options.means: The bus may keep waiting until the Province funds it.

options.label: No
options.means: No local money goes to a regional bus.

asks.title: How much should property taxes go up in 2027?
asks.why: Property taxes rose 12.8% in 2026. The draft 2027 budget starts at a 10.4% increase, and the new council decides it, with adoption expected early 2027 (last year: January 13).

options.label: Freeze them (no increase)
options.means: Services, repairs or projects get cut or delayed to make the budget balance.

options.label: Up by inflation only
options.means: Keeps the District’s buying power about the same; some new spending waits.

options.label: Above inflation if needed
options.means: Pays for growth, repairs and new services, with a bigger tax bill.

asks.title: How should Squamish speed up dike upgrades?
asks.why: Much of Squamish sits on a floodplain. The District raises dikes a section at a time, mostly when grants come through.

options.label: Borrow to go faster
options.means: Interest gets added to future tax bills.

options.label: Raise taxes to go faster
options.means: Higher tax bills now, no interest.

options.label: Keep waiting for grants
options.means: Cheapest for taxpayers, slowest to finish.
